claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a favorable strength–ductility combination.
Boron or carbon can serve as grain-boundary-pinning additions in the alloy.
Adding boron or carbon will cause grain-boundary pinning.
Adding boron or carbon will cause solute segregation at grain boundaries.
The pinning additions will reduce grain growth during thermal exposure.
The pinning additions will prevent the formation of brittle phases or precipitates during thermal exposure.
Suppressing grain growth and brittle phase or precipitate formation will maintain toughness under subsequent loading.
Suppressing grain growth and brittle phase or precipitate formation will maintain resistance to cracking under subsequent loading.
After identical thermal exposure and loading, the modified alloy will have greater toughness than the same alloy without the additions.
After identical thermal exposure and loading, the modified alloy will have greater resistance to cracking than the same alloy without the additions.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to exposure at approximately 500–700 °C for approximately 100 hours, followed by tensile or impact loading.
The optimal amount and type of grain-boundary-pinning addition may affect the outcome.
Interactions between the pinning additions and other alloying elements or impurities may affect the outcome.
